```{r}
m1

m2

scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")
scores
```

PART B

```{r}
scores[1, 2]

```

Question #3
```{r}
# class() returns numeric, which shows R simplifies a single row or column into a vector.
# R does this because a lone row or column has just one dimension left,
# and a vector works more smoothly with functions like mean() and sum().

#Question #4
# scores >= 90 still gives a logical matrix with names.
# scores[scores >= 90] picks scattered cellsby position,
# so they can't form a rectangle and come back as a plain vector without names.
# scores[1, ] keeps names because it takes a whole row, so the column names still apply.

```

```{r}
a <- matrix(1:4, nrow = 2)

a + b
a * b
a %*% b
```

Question #5
```{r}
#a * b multiplies matching cells ,
#so both matrices need the same dimensions.
#a %*% b is true matrix multiplication: each result cell is the sum of a row of a
#multiplied by a column of b, so the columns of a must match the rows of b.

#Question #6
#Transposing turns rows into columns and columns into rows .
#The names describe what each row or column holds, so they move with them:
#the old row names become the column names, and the old column names become the row names.
```

PART D
```{r}
scores_v2 <- cbind(scores, Dex = c(85, 91))
scores_v2

scores_v3 <- rbind(scores, Quiz3 = c(80, 88, 93))
scores_v3
```


Question #7
```{r}
#cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100)) gives a warning, not an error, and R drops the extra value.
#cbind() and rbind() need matching dimensions because a matrix must be a full rectangle, so #mismatched sizes would silently lose or repeat data.

#Question #8
#Use rbind() when each new batch of data is a new row with the same columns, like adding 
#each day's sales for the same products to a sales table.
#The columns stay fixed and only the rows grow over time.
```

Question #9 
```{r}
#dim(arr) gives three numbers: the number of rows, the number of columns, and the number of layers.
# For example, dim(arr) of 2 3 4 means 4 layers, each a 2 x 3 matrix.

#Question #10
#Quiz scores for 3 students across 2 quizzes, recorded over 4 weeks, fit a 3D array
# A single 2D matrix can only hold one week at a time, so it can't keep all the weeks together in #one structure.
```

PART F
```{r}
class_a <- matrix(c(85, 90, 78, 92), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                   dimnames = list(c("S1", "S2"), c("Midterm", "Final")))
class_b <- matrix(c(88, 84, 95, 91), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                   dimnames = list(c("S3", "S4"), c("Midterm", "Final")))

all_students <- rbind(class_a, class_b)
all_students

rowMeans(all_students)
```

Question #11
```{r}
#I chose rbind() because class_a and class_b have the same columns but different students.
#Shared column names meant the data described the same variables, so the new students belonged as extra rows.
#If the two matrices had shared row names with different score columns, cbind() would have been correct.

#I would stack all 5 matrices on top of each other, one after another, so every student becomes a #row in one matrix with the same 2 columns. To check it, dim() should show the total number of students and 2 columns.
```

Conclusion
```{r}
#A matrix is a 2D structure with rows and columns, while an array can have three or more #dimensions, such as rows, columns, and layers.
#Both hold only one data type, and a matrix is really just a 2D array.
#cbind() and rbind() are useful for growing a dataset over time, for example adding each new day's sales as a row with rbind(),
#or adding a new quiz as a column with cbind() for the same group of students.
```
